= Words to watch: contextual guidance for Malagasy translation =

== Source and status ==
Adapted from Wikipedia contributors,
[https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Words_to_watch&oldid=1382059772 Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch, revision 1382059772],
consulted 3 November 2026. Source revision/history credits its contributors.
Source and adapted material: Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0.
The examples below retain the source page's warning groups; Malagasy editorial
advice and illustrative equivalents are local adaptations, not official policy.

There are no forbidden words or expressions. These are caution signals for an
editorial decision, not a blacklist, censorship rule, exhaustive vocabulary or
case-insensitive replacement table. A legitimate technical/legal meaning can
justify a term. Review meaning and rhetoric in Malagasy equivalents too.

== Protected source wording ==
Do not apply caution-based replacement inside direct quotations, original work
titles, or citation metadata. Preserve those words accurately, including offensive
wording when necessary for faithful, relevant reproduction. A translated quote
must be clearly identified and preserve meaning/tone, not sanitize an opinion.
The exception protects source wording; it does not authorize gratuitous quotation,
plagiarism, unsupported allegations or presenting the source's judgment as fact.
Quoted attribution is not a loophole for promotion or undue weight.

== Puffery and peacock language ==
Examples: legendary, best, great, greatest, acclaimed, iconic, visionary,
outstanding, leading, celebrated, popular, award-winning, landmark, cutting-edge,
innovative, revolutionary, extraordinary, brilliant, hit, famous, renowned,
remarkable, prestigious, world-class, respected, notable, virtuoso, honorable,
awesome, unique, pioneering, phenomenal, prominent.

Replace unsupported praise/blame with specific supported facts. Name an actual
award, reception or measurable achievement instead of an unqualified superlative.
Malagasy words such as malaza or miavaka need the same contextual review, not
automatic removal; faithfully attribute evaluations that the article needs.

== Contentious labels ==
Examples: cult, racist, perverted, sexist, homophobic, transphobic, misogynistic,
sect, fundamentalist, heretic, extremist, denialist, terrorist, freedom fighter,
bigot, myth, -gate, pseudo-, controversial.

Do not insert value judgments or imply an established controversy from an
editor's choice of label. Use reliable-source support, context and clear
attribution for contentious characterizations, especially about living people.
Explain actual disputes rather than merely calling a subject controversial.
Do not confuse scholarly myth with a claim that a belief is false. Established
source-supported terms such as pseudoscience need not be concealed or softened.

== Unsupported attributions and weasel language ==
Examples: some people say, many people remember, many scholars state,
it is believed/regarded/considered, many are of the opinion, most feel,
experts declare, it is often reported, it is widely thought, research has shown,
science says, scientists claim, it is often said, officially, is widely regarded as,
X has been described as Y.

Identify who said/believes a claim and what supports it. Do not replace an
identified source with an invented consensus or anonymous authority. A summary
in a lead can be justified by precise attribution in the body; these phrases are
not automatically wrong. Malagasy misy milaza and heverina fa merit the same
check for real, identifiable support.

== Expressions of doubt and scare quotes ==
Examples: supposed, apparent, purported, alleged, accused, so-called;
scare quotes such as a Yale "report", and undue emphasis such as a Baptist church
with only Baptist emphasized.

Do not insinuate doubt through typography or loaded wording. Conversely, retain
genuine source-supported uncertainty and legal distinctions: an accusation is
not a conviction. Attribute the allegation instead of presenting it as fact.
Use the equivalent of called for an ordinary name, not an unjustified so-called.

== Editorializing and implied relationships ==
Examples: notably, it should be noted, arguably, interestingly, essentially,
utterly, actually, only, clearly, absolutely, of course, without a doubt, indeed,
happily, sadly, tragically, aptly, fortunately, unfortunately, untimely.
Additional source-discussed warning examples: fundamentally, basically, just,
obviously, naturally. Relationship words: but, despite, however, though, although,
furthermore, while.

Do not instruct readers how to feel or assume their expectations/knowledge.
Prefer supported facts to announcing significance. Transition words are not
forbidden: ensure they do not invent contradiction, causation, surprise or an
evaluative relationship between independently sourced facts. In Malagasy review
mazava ho azy, indrisy, soa ihany and similar expressions for these effects.

== Loaded substitutes for said ==
Examples: reveal, point out, clarify, expose, explain, find, note, observe, insist,
speculate, surmise, claim, assert, admit, confess, deny, confirm.

Prefer a neutral attributed statement when the source only establishes that
someone spoke/wrote it. Do not imply truth, discovery, guilt or unreliability by
varying the reporting verb for style. Said, described, wrote, commented, remarked,
according to and usually stated can be neutral in appropriate contexts. A genuine
documented confession or denial may be described precisely; do not erase it just
because its verb is on this list.

== Euphemisms ==
Examples: passed away, gave their life, eternal rest, make love, challenge,
an issue with, collateral damage, differently abled.

Use clear, accurate, respectful language, not rhetoric that hides death, injury,
disability or responsibility. In relevant sourced prose maty can be more precise
than an unexamined euphemism for death. Do not assume every medical/disability
term is inappropriate or impose a clinical claim not present in the evidence.

== Cliches and idioms ==
Examples: lion's share, tip of the iceberg, landslide, white elephant,
gild the lily, take the plunge, ace up the sleeve, bird in the hand, twist of fate,
at the end of the day, rounded out the top five, the likes of.

Translate the intended literal meaning, not a source idiom word-for-word.
Use a supported proportion, margin, event or action rather than a rhetorical
comparison. A literal discussion of an iceberg is not an idiom violation.

== Relative time ==
Examples: recently, lately, currently, today, presently, to date, X years ago,
formerly, in the past, traditionally, this/last/next (year/month/winter/spring/
summer/fall/autumn), yesterday, tomorrow, in the future, now, to this day, soon,
since.

Use supported explicit dates/periods and dated status claims where possible.
Do not invent a precise date absent from sources or silently update a quote.
Consider hemisphere/calendar differences when a season is used. Traditions and
technical terms such as recent in geology require their actual contextual sense.
Malagasy ankehitriny, vao haingana and hatramin' izao need the same dated context.

== Unspecified places or events ==
Examples: this country, here, there, somewhere, sometimes, often, occasionally,
somehow.

State the evidenced place, time, frequency or mechanism. Do not assume a Malagasy
reader shares the source author's country or viewpoint. Do not manufacture
precision when a source gives only a qualified/general statement.

== Obituary-style survived by ==
Examples: is/was survived by, [Name]'s survivors include.

Prefer a sourced account of family and chronology, not a newspaper-obituary
formula. Do not infer that all children or relatives were listed or that absent
relatives had died. Preserve such phrases in actual quotations or source titles.

== Person versus office ==
Distinguish a named person from the institution or position, and their office at
the time of an event from their later status. Attribute constitutional powers to
the office rather than its current holder; date claims about officeholders. Do
not write former president for an event during the person's presidency merely
because they have left office by the time of translation.

== Neologisms and new compounds ==
Source-discussed examples include pre-, post-, non-, anti-, -like, -ism, -ist,
abortionism, evolutionism, lesbianism, transgenderism.

Do not invent unstable technical vocabulary or ideological labels. Use a
reliable established meaning, or a precise descriptive Malagasy explanation
labelled honestly in vocabulary evidence. A productive prefix/suffix is not
automatically wrong, but must not manufacture a doctrine, stigma or consensus.

== Easily confused terms ==
Examples discussed in the source: Arab, Arabic, Arabian, Islamic, Muslim,
Islamist, Middle-eastern, Muslim Arab.

Keep language, script, geography, ethnicity, religion and ideology distinct;
similar spelling or overlap of populations does not make the terms synonyms.
Apply the same care to scientific, historical and cultural distinctions in
Malagasy. When the intended sense cannot be established, retain a blocker.

== Vulgarities, obscenities, and profanities ==
No automatic censorship. Preserve relevant verbatim quotations and original
titles/names without replacing characters with asterisks or euphemisms. In the
article's own voice, include offensive wording only when needed for accuracy
and relevance (for example, the expression itself is the subject), not for shock.

== Review procedure, not a token filter ==
For each material occurrence outside protected source wording, consider the
intended sense, reliable-source support, attribution, reader clarity, and effect
of the Malagasy phrasing. Rewrite only when it improves accuracy/neutrality.
Record significant decisions in notes.wiki and the existing neutrality/citations/
terminology gates. Do not add a forbidden-word regex, blanket deletion, or automatic
censorship of source metadata. The examples are not an instruction to fetch the
linked guides, sources or dictionaries repeatedly; normal network limits apply.
